desc:
Each node of a binary tree holds some coins, and the total number of coins in the tree equals the number of nodes. In one move you take one coin from a node and give it to an adjacent node (its parent or one of its children).

Return the minimum number of moves after which every node holds exactly one coin.

How trees are given. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order (top to bottom, left to right). The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn; a missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped.

For example, [1,2,3,-1,4] is the tree whose root 1 has children 2 and 3; node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child; node 3 is a leaf.

Here the numbers in the array are the coin counts of the nodes.

Example 1

tree = [3,0,0]
Output: 2
Move one coin to each child.

Example 2

tree = [0,3,0]
Output: 3
The left child sends two coins to the root (2 moves) and the root passes one of them on to the right child (1 move).
constraints: The sum of all node values equals the number of nodes
The array follows the encoding above exactly
hints: Consider one edge between a node and its child. Only the coins that must cross this edge matter, and you can ignore what happens inside the two sides.

Look at the subtree below the edge. It owns coins coins and has size nodes, so it needs size - coins coins from outside (or has coins - size to send out). That many coins must cross the edge, in whichever direction.

Every crossing costs exactly one move, and crossings on different edges never help each other, so the answer is the sum over all non-root nodes of |coins(subtree) - size(subtree)|. Compute it bottom-up with one running 'excess' per node.
editorial: Define the excess of a node u as excess(u) = coins in subtree(u) - nodes in subtree(u). If it is positive, that many coins have to leave the subtree through the edge to the parent; if it is negative, that many must come in. Either way the edge between u and its parent is used exactly |excess(u)| times, and no sequence of moves can use it fewer times.

The bound is achievable by moving coins greedily from the leaves upwards, so the answer is the sum of |excess(u)| over all non-root nodes. The excess recurrence is excess(u) = val[u] - 1 + excess(left) + excess(right). A backwards sweep over the level-order array gives O(n) time and O(n) memory. Since the root's own excess is always 0 (coins equal nodes), summing over all nodes gives the same total.
